title: BCO Lead Automation
summary: An n8n + Apify pipeline that scrapes Ottawa tech-company directories and Google Maps into a scored lead list for Builders Collective Ottawa sponsorship outreach.
html:
Overview

A lead-generation automation pipeline built for Builders Collective Ottawa (BCO), a community/sponsorship-driven org, to build a scored list of Ottawa-area tech companies worth approaching for sponsorship. It's not a web app — it's a self-hosted n8n instance orchestrating scraper actors that feed a shared Google Sheet.

Problem

Finding and qualifying sponsorship-worthy tech companies in Ottawa by hand — checking member directories, searching maps by category, cross-referencing who's already been contacted — doesn't scale past a handful of leads at a time. (draft — confirm) The goal was an automated first pass that builds a deduplicated, scored candidate list, leaving the human judgment (relevance, sponsorship capacity, personalized outreach) for after the raw list exists.

What I built

  • A self-hosted n8n instance (Docker Compose, forked from a local n8n template) running two workflows on manual triggers
  • Directory scraper workflow: pulls the Kanata North Business Association member directory, Invest Ottawa's company list, and the Ottawa Board of Trade tech directory via Apify actors, normalizes results, and appends them to a Raw - Directories sheet
  • Google Maps scraper workflow: runs 6 category searches (software, AI, cybersecurity, cloud, telecom, robotics) via an Apify Google Maps actor, capped at 20 results each (~120 max) with contact enrichment/reviews/images deliberately disabled to control Apify's per-result cost, appending to Raw - Google Maps
  • Both workflows dedupe and upsert into a shared Master Leads sheet using a Dedup Key, with manual scoring columns (BCO Relevance, Sponsorship Capacity, Ottawa Presence, Community Signal → Priority Score) for a human to fill in afterward
  • A GCP project holding the service account/OAuth credentials and IAM permissions that let n8n read and write the shared Google Sheet
  • BCO Leads 2.0: a Claude Code–built enrichment pass on top of the raw V1 scrape — per-company contact emails, personalization hooks, and outreach-status tracking, covering the KNBA and Invest Ottawa lead sets
  • The V1 n8n workflows themselves were built with Claude and Cursor as AI pair-programmers for the workflow/config authoring

Architecture

n8n (Docker Compose, port 5678, persistent n8n_data volume) is the orchestration layer. Each workflow calls out to Apify actors via HTTP request nodes — one hitting a general web-scraper actor against directory pages, the other hitting a Google Maps scraper actor — using APIFY_TOKEN. Results are normalized in n8n, filtered (directory results by tech keywords; maps results by category), and written to Google Sheets (BCO_GOOGLE_SHEET_ID) via upsert nodes keyed on a computed dedup key. Access to that sheet is governed by a GCP project — service account credentials and IAM permissions scoped to the Sheets API — rather than a personal Google account, so read/write access to Master Leads can be managed and revoked independently of any one person's login. Both workflows are manually triggered, not scheduled — this is a run-on-demand pipeline, not a fully autonomous one.

Currently two disconnected halves: the checked-in SETUP_README.md is explicit that this V1 pipeline does not find individual employees, enrich contact details, draft emails, or send outreach. A separate folder in the repo (Recovered KNBA and Invest Ottawa files/) does contain exactly that — contact emails, personalization hooks, outreach status per company — produced by BCO Leads 2.0, a Claude Code–driven enrichment pass run independently of the n8n workflows. The scraping automation (V1) and the enrichment work (2.0) aren't wired together into one pipeline yet.

Decisions

  • n8n + Apify over a custom scraper — (draft — confirm) let the pipeline reuse battle-tested scraper actors (web + Google Maps) instead of writing and maintaining scraping/anti-bot logic from scratch, at the cost of Apify's per-run pricing.
  • Manual triggers over a schedule — (draft — confirm) kept the pipeline run-on-demand while still validating the approach, rather than scheduling runs before knowing the data was actually useful.
  • Capping Google Maps results and disabling enrichment per search — a deliberate cost control: 20 results × 6 categories keeps the Apify bill predictable while still giving broad category coverage.

Results

A working, repeatable pipeline that produces a deduplicated Master Leads sheet from two independent sources (member directories + Google Maps), ready for manual scoring. (draft — confirm actual lead counts / how many have been contacted so far)

What I learned

  • Splitting "find candidates" from "qualify and personalize" into separate stages made it possible to ship the scraping half without having solved contact-enrichment yet. (draft — confirm)
  • Deliberately disabling expensive Apify enrichment options up front (reviews, images, contact details) kept early iteration cheap while the workflow shape was still changing. (draft — confirm)

What's next

  • Connect BCO Leads 2.0's Claude Code enrichment pass back into the automated V1 pipeline so scraping and enrichment run as one flow
  • Consider moving from manual triggers to a schedule once the workflow shape is settled

title: Brain Tumor Detection Model
summary: A CNN that classifies glioma vs. healthy brain MRI slices, with Grad-CAM heatmaps so the prediction is explainable, not just a label.
html:
Overview

A deep learning pipeline that classifies MRI slices as glioma vs. healthy, trained on the UCSF-PDGM collection from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA). (draft — confirm) The project isn't just a classifier: it also produces Grad-CAM heatmaps so a prediction comes with a visual explanation of which region of the brain drove it, rather than a bare label.

Problem

Tumor screening from MRI is slow and reviewer-dependent, and a black-box classifier that just outputs "glioma" or "healthy" isn't trustworthy enough to reason about — there's no way to check why the model thinks what it thinks. (draft — confirm) The goal was a model that's both accurate and inspectable.

What I built

  • A CNN image classifier trained on central MRI slices extracted from DICOM/NIfTI volumes (data_prep.py, make_dataset.py)
  • A training pipeline with data augmentation for robustness and automatic best-checkpoint saving (train.py, model.py)
  • An evaluation pass reporting precision, recall, F1, and a precision–recall curve (evaluate.py)
  • Grad-CAM heatmap generation to visualize which brain regions influenced each prediction (grad_cam.py)

Architecture

Raw MRI volumes (DICOM/NIfTI) go through data_prep.py, which extracts central slices and converts them into NumPy arrays (X.npy/y.npy). train.py loads those arrays, does a stratified 70/15/15 train/val/test split, and fits a CNN:

  • 3 conv blocks (32 → 64 → 128 filters, 3×3, ReLU, same padding) each followed by 2×2 max-pooling, over a single-channel 224×224 input
  • Flatten → Dense(128, ReLU) → Dropout(0.5) → Dense(1, sigmoid) for binary glioma-vs-healthy output
  • Adam optimizer (lr 1e-4), binary crossentropy, trained up to 40 epochs with EarlyStopping (patience 5 on val_loss) and ModelCheckpoint saving the best weights to models/best_model.h5
  • Light augmentation on the training set only: ±10° rotation, 5% width/height shift, 10% zoom, horizontal flip; batch size 16

evaluate.py and grad_cam.py both load a saved checkpoint — one to score it against the held-out test split, the other to render heatmaps for individual predictions.

Decisions

  • Central-slice extraction over full 3D volumes — trades some spatial context for a much smaller, faster-to-train 2D CNN (single-channel 224×224 input) than a volumetric model would need, which mattered more for a first working version than squeezing out volumetric accuracy.
  • A deliberately simple 3-block CNN over a pretrained backbone — (draft — confirm) kept the model small and fast to iterate on for a first version, at the cost of whatever accuracy a transfer-learned backbone might have added.
  • Grad-CAM instead of a plain classifier — treats interpretability as a first-class requirement rather than an afterthought, since a medical-imaging prediction without a "why" is hard to trust or debug.

Results

Evaluation reports precision, recall, F1-score, and a precision–recall curve on the held-out test split (see evaluate.py output for exact numbers — not captured in this note). (draft — confirm actual metrics)

What I learned

  • Interpretability tooling (Grad-CAM) is worth building alongside the model, not bolted on after — it changed how I debugged misclassifications during training.
  • Medical imaging formats (DICOM/NIfTI) need real preprocessing discipline before they're usable as flat training arrays. (draft — confirm)

Future improvements

  • Multi-modal MRI input (T1, T1-CE, T2, FLAIR) instead of a single sequence
  • 3D CNN models trained on full MRI volumes instead of central slices
  • Clinical label prediction (e.g. IDH mutation status)

title: CRA Audit Knowledge Retrieval
summary: The retrieval foundation (semantic + keyword + graph) for a planned future RAG system over a hand-curated vault of CRA audit-methodology notes — not yet shipped; generation is still to come.
html:
Overview

A work-in-progress project to build a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) system over a hand-curated knowledge base of Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) audit methodology: organization structure, audit-methodology practices, statistics, software-controls, risk-control frameworks, and 6 public audit/evaluation case studies, sourced from official canada.ca documentation rather than any forum or community content. Current state: retrieval foundation only, not shipped — the hybrid retrieval layer (semantic + keyword + graph) is built and evaluated, but the generation step that would make this a complete RAG system hasn't been built yet; today a query returns ranked, explained source notes, not a synthesized answer. It's also worth being upfront that the retrieval code (rag/, eval/) is currently local-only and not yet pushed to the public GitHub repo, which today only reflects the earlier vault-content commits.

Problem

Public CRA audit documentation is comprehensive but scattered across many separate official pages and methodology documents — finding the right source note for a specific audit question means either already knowing where to look or manually searching each source. (draft — confirm) The goal was a retrieval layer that could surface the most relevant, properly-sourced notes for a question, with a transparent explanation of why each result was ranked where it was — not a black-box answer, since audit findings need to be traceable to their source.

What I built

  • A hand-curated Obsidian vault of ~444 markdown notes (~289 substantive, ~155 infrastructure/index notes) organized into numbered folders (00-Start through 99-Sources), each source note carrying YAML frontmatter with source_url, publisher, and accessed_on pointing back to the originating canada.ca page
  • corpus.py / chunking.py: walk the vault and split notes into retrieval-sized chunks
  • embeddings.py: embed chunks locally with sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (no API key or per-call cost) into a flat NumPy array used directly as the vector store — no external vector DB service
  • lexical.py: a parallel BM25 keyword index (rank-bm25) for exact-term matching semantic search can miss
  • graph.py: a networkx graph built from the vault's own note-to-note wikilinks (Obsidian-style double-bracket links between notes), used for n-hop graph-proximity expansion
  • retrieve.py: blends semantic similarity, BM25 score, graph proximity, and an authoritative-source bonus into one weighted hybrid score, with a why_included explanation attached to every result
  • A CLI (python -m rag.cli {index|search|stats}) as the only interface — no web UI or chat interface yet
  • A real evaluation harness (eval/retrieval_eval.py, eval/questions.json — 10 hand-written Q&A pairs with expected notes) computing Hit@1/3/5, Recall@5/10, and MRR across multiple retrieval modes

Architecture

Vault markdown (vault/public/...-style folder structure, curated by hand) → corpus.py/chunking.py build chunked documents → embeddings.py produces a local NumPy embedding matrix (rag_data/embeddings.npy) while lexical.py builds a BM25 index (rag_data/lexical_bm25.pkl) and graph.py builds a wikilink graph (rag_data/graph.json) in parallel. retrieve.py queries all three signals plus a source-authority bonus and combines them into a single ranked, explained result list, exposed only via the CLI. No LLM is called anywhere in the pipeline.

Decisions

  • Local embeddings over an API-based embedding model — sentence-transformers running locally means no per-query cost and no external dependency, at the cost of lower embedding quality than a larger hosted model.
  • A flat NumPy array over a dedicated vector database — (draft — confirm) reasonable at the current corpus size (~289 substantive notes); would need revisiting if the corpus grew by an order of magnitude.
  • Hybrid retrieval (semantic + BM25 + graph) over semantic search alone — combines what embeddings are good at (conceptual similarity) with what BM25 is good at (exact term matches embeddings can miss) and what the graph adds (notes the author explicitly linked as related), rather than betting on one signal.
  • Building and proving out retrieval before generation — the plan is a full RAG system, but getting hybrid retrieval right first (and evaluating it) means the eventual generation step will be grounded in results already shown to be accurate, rather than layering an LLM on top of unproven retrieval over audit-sensitive content.

Results

On the 10-question hand-written eval set, the hybrid_graph retrieval mode reaches Hit@1 = 0.9 and MRR = 0.91 — strong on this small set, but 10 questions is not a statistically robust benchmark and shouldn't be read as a general accuracy number.

What I learned

  • Building the eval harness alongside the retrieval pipeline (rather than after) made it possible to actually compare hybrid vs. single-signal retrieval modes with real numbers instead of eyeballing results. (draft — confirm)
  • Combining three different retrieval signals (semantic, lexical, graph) surfaced results that no single signal would have ranked as highly on its own. (draft — confirm with a concrete example)

What's next

  • Build the generation layer on top of this retrieval foundation — an LLM that answers a question using the retrieved, source-traceable notes as grounding — to complete the planned RAG implementation
  • Commit the rag/ and eval/ retrieval code so the public repo reflects the actual current state of the project
  • Grow the eval question set beyond 10 questions for a more robust accuracy signal

title: Eco Intelligence Dashboard
summary: A Next.js admin dashboard, based on the open-source TailAdmin template, built for TechnataHack24 to monitor router activity, energy savings, and heat management.
html:
Overview

The frontend of Eco Intelligence, built for the TechnataHack24 hackathon: intended as a dashboard giving IT administrators a real-time view of router activity, energy savings, and heat/thermal management, per the project README. Important caveat (draft — confirm/rewrite): the committed code in this repo is substantially the stock TailAdmin free Next.js admin dashboard template — the repo carries TailAdmin's own screenshot (tailadmin-nextjs.jpg) and an IDE module file named free-nextjs-admin-dashboard.iml, and the homepage (src/app/page.tsx) still renders a generic <ECommerce /> component under the title "Eco-Intelligence - User Dashboard" rather than router/energy-specific widgets. No GSAP dependency or usage exists anywhere in the codebase despite the README mentioning it (the actual animation library is Framer Motion), and no axios/fetch calls to a backend API were found in the pages searched. This note is written from the README's stated intent — please correct whichever parts describe the template's default state rather than what was actually customized for the hackathon (e.g. was a real router/energy dashboard built on top of this scaffold elsewhere, or is this repo's committed state the full extent of it?).

Problem

IT infrastructure teams don't have a simple, live view of how much energy their network hardware is actually consuming, or when equipment is running hot — so energy waste and overheating both go unnoticed until they're expensive. (draft — confirm; this is the README's stated problem, not verified against custom code in this repo)

What I built

  • Scaffolded a Next.js admin dashboard from the TailAdmin template as the starting point for an IT energy/heat monitoring tool
  • (draft — confirm) Router activity, energy-saving estimates, and heat management views — described in the README but not found as distinct components in this repo's committed source; may have been built elsewhere, planned but not finished, or since removed
  • Chart-driven views (ApexCharts, already part of the TailAdmin base) available for presenting time-series data
  • Animated, responsive UI via Framer Motion

Architecture

Next.js (App Router) frontend styled with Tailwind CSS, charting via react-apexcharts, transitions via Framer Motion — the TailAdmin template's standard stack. The README describes a REST API connection to a separate backend serving router status and energy/heat predictions, but no such integration was found in the pages searched in this repo. (draft — confirm actual data source, if any is wired up)

Decisions

  • TailAdmin as a starting scaffold over a from-scratch dashboard — (draft — confirm) let the team get a polished, chart-ready admin UI in place immediately under hackathon time pressure, rather than spending hackathon hours on dashboard-shell plumbing.

Results

Submitted for TechnataHack24. (draft — confirm what was actually demoed/judged, given the gap between the README's description and this repo's committed state, and any placement/award results)

What I learned

title: Happy Hour In My City
summary: A restaurant happy-hour discovery site — browse deals, filter on a map, and (eventually) manage listings as a business owner.
html:
Overview

Happy Hour In My City (happyhourinmycity.com) is a restaurant happy-hour discovery site: browse and filter deals by location on a map, with a directory of participating businesses. It's built as a Next.js app with a public-facing consumer product that's real and live, plus an early-stage owner/admin management layer.

Problem

Happy hour deals are scattered across individual restaurant sites and social posts — there's no single place to discover what's on, where, and when, filtered by location. (draft — confirm) The goal was a directory-and-map product where a diner could find nearby deals at a glance, and eventually where a restaurant owner could self-manage their own listing instead of relying on someone else to keep it current.

What I built

  • A public discovery experience: home page with hero, listings, and a map section, plus /about, /mission, /faq (split into user and business FAQs), /join-restaurant, and /recommend for growing the directory
  • Auth and account flows (/login, /signup) backed by Supabase, with role-gating middleware that checks a profiles table (role, approval_status, business_id) to protect /owner/* and /admin/* routes
  • An Airtable-backed content API (/businesses) pulling Businesses/Offers/Recurring Rules tables, with a 343-line local mock-data fallback so the app still runs without Airtable credentials in dev
  • Map display via @vis.gl/react-google-maps, with geocoding routed through the free Nominatim API instead of paid Google Geocoding to control cost
  • Legal/support pages (/disclaimer, /privacy, /terms), an offline PWA fallback page, and Capacitor scaffolding for a future native app wrapper (not yet initialized)
  • PostHog and Vercel Analytics wired in for usage tracking

Architecture

Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) with Tailwind v4 and shadcn/radix-ui components. Content lives in Airtable rather than a traditional database — the /businesses API route fetches Businesses/Offers/Recurring Rules via Airtable's REST API using AIRTABLE_BASE_ID/TABLE_NAME/TOKEN, falling back to bundled mock data when those env vars are absent (dev-friendly, but a hard error in production if missing). Supabase handles auth and session state (@supabase/ssr), with middleware gating owner/admin routes based on a profiles table. Map rendering uses the Google Maps JS API, but geocoding (converting addresses to coordinates) deliberately goes through free Nominatim rather than Google's paid geocoding endpoint.

Currently incomplete: despite the role-gating middleware being fully built for /owner/dashboard, /owner/pending-approval, and /admin/dashboard, the dashboard pages themselves are still 9-line stub pages — a heading and one sentence, no actual management UI yet.

Decisions

  • Airtable over a traditional database for content — (draft — confirm) lets non-technical people (or the founder without touching code) edit business/offer data directly in a spreadsheet-like tool, at the cost of a REST round-trip and Airtable's own rate limits.
  • Nominatim over paid Google Geocoding — a deliberate cost-avoidance choice: the Google Maps key is scoped to JS map display only, keeping the app's per-request cost down while it's pre-revenue.
  • Building the role-gating middleware before the dashboards it protects — sets up the access-control contract (who can see /owner/* and /admin/*) ahead of time, so the dashboard UI can be built directly against a working permission system rather than retrofitting auth later.

Results

Live public-facing site with real discovery, business-directory, and account flows; happyhourinmycity.com and its register. subdomain appear as active links across the site and social channels (Instagram/TikTok @happyhourinmycity). (draft — confirm traffic/usage numbers, if any worth citing)

What I learned

  • Scoping paid APIs carefully (Google Maps for display only, free Nominatim for geocoding) matters a lot for a pre-revenue local-discovery product where per-request cost adds up fast at scale. (draft — confirm)
  • Building the permission layer (Supabase role/approval gating) ahead of the UI it protects made it a clear, testable contract rather than something bolted on after the dashboards existed. (draft — confirm)

What's next

  • Build out the actual owner and admin dashboard UI — currently placeholder pages despite the access-control layer being ready
  • Decide on and resolve the static-export vs. server-route conflict blocking Capacitor native app packaging

title: NSE Stock Tracker
summary: A Streamlit app for exploring NSE (Indian exchange) stocks live — pricing, financials, and news pulled through the Yahoo Finance API.
html:
Overview

An interactive stock market tracker for NSE (National Stock Exchange, India) stocks, built with Streamlit and the Yahoo Finance API (yfinance). Co-built with Mark Allen while in grade XII at Arsha Vidya Mandir — one of the earliest real projects I shipped.

Problem

Understanding a stock's full picture (price history, financials, holders, analyst opinion, news) usually means jumping between several different tools and sites. The goal was one interface where picking a ticker gives access to all of that in one place, built to be understandable by people who aren't already market experts.

What I built

  • A ticker selector pulling the live NSE F&O stock list, feeding ~17 selectable features: stock summary, general info, historical data, price/volume plots, a calculator, major holders, balance sheet, cash flow, earnings, financials, actions, sustainability, analyst recommendations, earnings calendar, and latest news
  • Interactive price/volume charts (Plotly) with a configurable timeframe (from 1-minute to 3-month periods)
  • CSV export of any pulled dataset
  • A basic username/password login and sign-up module (SQLite-backed) gating access to the sidebar
  • A HTML-embedded navbar linking out to a companion YouTube playlist teaching stock market basics, aimed at the same beginner audience

Architecture

A single Streamlit app (Stock_Market_Tracker_Original.py) drives the whole experience: a sidebar ticker selector and feature selector, both backed by live calls to yfinance.Ticker(...). Selected data is rendered through pandas/Plotly directly in the page. A separate About.py Streamlit page carries the project's own writeup. A SQLite database (acc.db, via sqlite3) backs a simple userdetails table (username/password) for login and sign-up, checked against st.sidebar.button("Login") / st.sidebar.button("Sign Up").

Decisions

  • AlphaVantage → Yahoo Finance for data — AlphaVantage's free tier gated most of the interesting data behind a paywall; Yahoo Finance was free and unrestricted, so we switched early once that became clear.
  • Tkinter → Streamlit for the UI — Tkinter's learning curve and verbosity for even simple widgets made it a poor fit for two beginners; Streamlit replaced it (and absorbed what Matplotlib/pandas were doing for visualization) with far less code and a much shorter path to a working UI.

Results

A working, deployable Streamlit app covering the full range of stock research features listed above, live against real NSE market data. (draft — confirm any deployment/usage numbers)

What I learned

  • Picking the right tool early (Streamlit over Tkinter, Yahoo Finance over AlphaVantage) mattered more than pushing through with the first choice — both pivots came from hitting a real wall, not from over-planning upfront.
  • This was an early lesson in scoping: a "track everything about a stock" feature list is easy to say and a lot of surface area to actually build. (draft — confirm)

title: Route Optimizer
summary: A real-time route optimization app with a live traffic map, an AI chat assistant, and Solace-powered live messaging — built for Uottahacks7.
html:
Overview

A route optimization app built at Uottahacks7: a live map interface showing routes and traffic markers, an LLM-backed recommendation engine (Groq) that reasons about a route's traffic conditions, and a Solace PubSub+ connection that keeps the client aware of its real-time connection status for live updates.

Problem

Standard route-planning UIs show a route but not why it's a good one, and they don't adapt cleanly to live traffic conditions changing mid-trip. The goal was a route optimizer that treats traffic as a live signal driving the route, not a one-time input, and gives the user a conversational way to ask about it. (draft — confirm)

What I built

  • An interactive map (Leaflet) rendering routes and live traffic markers (Map.tsx, RouteMarkers.tsx, TrafficMarker.tsx)
  • A route panel presenting the optimized path and its details (RoutePanel.tsx)
  • An embedded chatbot widget for conversational trip assistance (ChatBotWidget.css, chatbot edge function)
  • A useSolaceConnection hook (SolaceConnection.tsx) that manages the Solace PubSub+ connection lifecycle client-side and surfaces connect/error state via toast notifications, backed by a get-solace-config edge function that hands the client its connection config
  • A Supabase edge function (optimize-route) that sends the current route and traffic data to Groq's mixtral-8x7b-32768 model and returns structured recommendations (alternative routes, expected delay severity, weather impact), with a safe default response if the Groq call fails

Architecture

React (Vite + TypeScript) frontend, styled with Tailwind and shadcn-ui, rendering the map via Leaflet. Three Supabase edge functions provide the backend: optimize-route builds a prompt from the route/traffic payload and calls the Groq chat completions API for recommendations, get-solace-config hands the client its Solace connection config, and chatbot serves the AI assistant. On the client, useSolaceConnection establishes and monitors the Solace connection so the UI can reflect real-time connectivity state.

Decisions

  • Supabase Edge Functions over a standalone backend — (draft — confirm) kept the whole stack deployable from one place under hackathon time pressure, without standing up separate backend infrastructure.
  • An LLM (Groq) for route recommendations instead of a hand-written optimization algorithm — turns route/traffic data into natural-language-derived recommendations (alternatives, delay severity, weather impact) without building a routing/optimization engine from scratch, at the cost of recommendations being only as reliable as the model's parsing of its own prompt response.
  • A safe fallback response when the Groq call fails or times out — the edge function always returns a 200 with a default recommendation rather than surfacing an error to the user, prioritizing a working demo over surfacing failures.

Results

Shipped as a working demo for Uottahacks7 combining live map routing, an LLM-driven recommendation engine, and Solace-backed real-time connectivity in one app. (draft — confirm placement/award results)

What I learned

  • Prompting an LLM for structured output (route alternatives, delay severity, weather impact) and then parsing that back out of free text is fragile — the edge function's fallback logic exists because that parsing can't be fully trusted. (draft — confirm)
  • Wiring a pub/sub layer (Solace) into a frontend app was new territory compared to typical request/response APIs, and changed how the UI had to be structured to react to connection-state changes rather than just fetch results. (draft — confirm)

title: International Tax Administration Complexity Dashboard
summary: A Power BI dashboard ranking tax administration burden across economies, built on a custom weighted score derived from World Bank Doing Business indicators.
html:
Overview

A data analytics project comparing tax compliance burden across international economies, built entirely on public World Bank Doing Business "Paying Taxes" data. Python and pandas clean, merge, and score the raw indicators; Power BI turns the result into a comparative, rankable dashboard.

Problem

Tax compliance burden varies a lot by jurisdiction — some economies demand more filing time, more separate payments per year, or a higher total tax rate — but there was no single transparent, reproducible score that combined those three signals into one ranking. The project answers: which economies in the dataset appear to have the most complex tax administration burden, based on public World Bank indicators?

What I built

  • A cleaning pipeline (merge_and_clean.py) that pulls three separate World Bank CSVs (PAY.TAX.TM, PAY.TAX.PYMT.FREQ.NO, PAY.TAX.TOT.TAX.RT.ZS), extracts the 2019 column from each, and merges them into one analytical dataset
  • Min-max normalization of each indicator into comparable 0–100 sub-scores (time_score, payments_score, tax_rate_score) in scoring.py
  • A weighted composite Tax Complexity Score: 0.40 * time_score + 0.30 * payments_score + 0.30 * tax_rate_score
  • Classification of economies into complexity bands based on that score
  • A Power BI dashboard for ranking, comparison, and stakeholder-facing visualization

Architecture

Three raw World Bank CSVs → merge_and_clean.py (pandas: select the 2019 column from each, inner-join on country, coerce numeric types, drop missing rows) → data/processed/tax_complexity_dashboard_ready.csv → scoring.py (min-max normalization + weighted composite score + banding into Low/Medium/High/Very High) → the processed CSV feeds a Power BI .pbix dashboard for the final visual layer.

Decisions

  • A transparent weighted formula over a black-box model — the 40/30/30 weighting is visible and adjustable, which matters for a dashboard meant to be defensible to stakeholders, not just accurate.
  • Min-max normalization per indicator before combining — the three raw indicators are on incompatible scales (hours, count, percent), so each is rescaled to 0–100 before the composite score is computed, keeping any one indicator from dominating by scale alone.

Results

Produces a ranked, banded comparison of tax administration complexity across every economy with complete 2019 data on all three indicators, visualized in an interactive Power BI dashboard (see images/dashboard_preview.png in the repo). In the processed output, Venezuela ranks highest at a complexity score of 63.5 ("High" band, driven by a 100/100 payments-frequency score); no economy in the dataset reaches the "Very High" band (75+).

What I learned

  • A single composite score is only as trustworthy as its weighting is explainable — keeping the formula simple and visible mattered more than squeezing out marginal accuracy. (draft — confirm)
  • Working from three independently-sourced World Bank CSVs surfaced real messiness (missing years, inconsistent coverage) that a clean single dataset wouldn't have — the pipeline settles on a single fixed year (2019) across all three rather than each indicator's own latest year, which keeps the comparison apples-to-apples but means the dashboard isn't automatically current. (draft — confirm whether a rolling "latest year" version is worth building)
